picks.title: UNCOVER/MegaScience Finds Uniform and Highly Bursty Star Formation at 3 < z < 9, Consistent with the High-redshift UV Luminosity Function
picks.abstract: Star formation timescales are key to understanding fundamental physics like feedback mechanisms, as well as the abundance of bright galaxies at z > 10. We investigate galaxy star formation histories (SFHs) and their evolution across z ∼ 3–9 by measuring the line-to-UV ratio ( R line ) and line equivalent width (EW) of H α +[N ii ] and [O iii ]+H β directly from UNCOVER/MegaScience spectro-photometry without relying on a specific SFH or nebular line modeling. Our photometric measurements recover R line and EW to <10% systematic accuracy compared to spectroscopy. This allows us to construct a large mass- (and flux-) complete sample and quantitatively examine how R line evolves with redshift and stellar mass. We find that the intrinsic scatter in R line does not significantly evolve with redshift across 3 < z < 7, though it may increase at z ≳ 8. We build population-level toy models using fsps to help interpret our observations, and find that scatter in R line primarily reflects the amplitude of SFH fluctuations; this implies that our observed lack of evolution in the scatter of R line is due to similar star formation burstiness from z ∼ 3 to z ∼ 7. Our observations are best reproduced by a set of SFHs with rising, long-duration, and large-amplitude bursts. Finally, we demonstrate that the toy model that best describes our z ∼ 6 data can boost UV brightness by up to Δ M UV ∼ −2.0 mag compared with a 200 Myr constant SFH, and naturally produces a large number of galaxies at z > 10. This suggests that no significant evolution in star formation burstiness is required to explain the abundance of UV-bright galaxies at high redshift.

picks.title: Trapping 11 thousand atoms in a tweezer array generated by a single metasurface
picks.abstract: The scalability of physical qubit numbers is a central challenge toward a universal fault-tolerant quantum computer. Here, we robustly trap 11,000 individual atoms in a tweezer array, thereby enabling the available single atom resource above the 10,000-atom level for the first time in neutral atom quantum computation platforms. This advance is enabled by a single metasurface, approximately 2 cm in diameter, that generates the entire tweezer array without the need for microscope objectives, thereby maximizing laser-power efficiency. The large aperture ensures a working distance of about 1.5 cm, allowing the metasurface to be placed outside the vacuum cell and avoiding the technical complications of in-vacuum operation. We further characterize the randomly loaded atom array using the statistical theory of percolation phase transitions. This work takes an important first step toward a quantum computer at the 10,000-qubit scale.

picks.title: Statistical characterization of valley coupling in Si/SiGe quantum dots via g -factor measurements near a valley vortex
picks.abstract: The presence of low-energy valley excitations in Si/SiGe heterostructures often causes spin qubits to fail. It is therefore important to develop robust protocols for characterizing the valley coupling. Here, we show that realistically sized samplings of valley energy distributions tend to dramatically overestimate the average valley coupling. But we find that knowledge of the valley phase, in addition to the valley splitting, can significantly improve our estimates. Motivated by this understanding, we propose a novel method to probe the valley phase landscape across the quantum well using simple g-factor measurements. An important calibration step in this procedure is to measure g in a loop enclosing a valley vortex, where the valley phase winds by 2 π around a zero of the valley splitting. This proposal establishes an important new tool for probing spin qubits, and it can be implemented in current experiments.

picks.title: Mean-motion Resonances in the Accretion Disks of Active Galactic Nuclei
picks.abstract: Mean-motion resonances (MMRs) are a generic outcome of convergent migration for bodies embedded in accretion disks around a central mass. Long studied in planetary systems, the same phenomenon should occur for stellar-mass black holes (BHs) in the disks of active galactic nuclei (AGN). In this work, we derive simple analytic criteria describing when BH pairs are driven out of resonance, and use them to chart MMR stability across AGN parameter space, accounting for disruption from general-relativistic apsidal precession, hydrodynamic turbulence, and stellar stirring. Across plausible AGN disk models, we find three MBH mass regimes: (i) for M / M ⊙ ≳ 10 7.5 , first-order resonances are generically unstable; (ii) for M / M ⊙ ≲ 10 6.5 , stable MMRs are always present; and (iii) for 10 6.5 ≲ M / M ⊙ ≲ 10 7.5 , stability depends on disk mass flux, the summed mass of the orbiters, and the nuclear-cusp slope. When present, stable MMRs commonly occur between an inner anti-trap and an outer trap set by thermal torques, a region where embedded objects migrate outward in the disk. These results imply that high-mass AGN allow convergent migration to proceed to LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK)-band mergers largely without resonant chains, whereas low- and intermediate-mass AGN can host MMRs, with the potential to reshape merger pathways.

picks.title: Expanding Chemical Space Enables Data–Driven Structure–Activity Relationships in Cage Catalysis
picks.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
picks.abstract: Data-driven approaches are increasingly popular in catalysis, supplementing and even replacing traditional strategies that relied on empirical optimization. However, their application in the field of bioinspired cage catalysis remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the limited chemical space of known catalytically active cages. As a result, mechanistic insights are often obtained using computationally intensive DFT calculations on a handful of structurally similar cages. As chemical systems grow in complexity, this approach becomes impractical. Herein, we report a framework that significantly expedites the exploration of a much wider structural landscape while offering computational insights. This is made possible by a novel in situ experimental procedure─which circumvents the traditional time-consuming process of prepare, isolate, characterize, and test─coupled with data-driven methods to identify molecular features that govern activity. Using this approach, we experimentally explore 30 unique PdnL2n cages (n = 2–4) that mediate a nitro-aldol reaction with activities spanning over 4 orders of magnitude. Using this data set, a random forest model trained on molecular descriptors was developed to predict ΔG‡ (MAE of 0.4 kcal mol–1 and R2 = 0.9). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis highlighted geometric preorganization and electrostatic interactions within the cage as key determinants of catalytic efficiency. Moreover, DFT calculations on a selection of cages further validated these insights, indicating that meaningful mechanistic understanding can be achieved at significantly reduced computational cost. We anticipate that this integrated, screening, data-driven, mechanistic strategy will provide a blueprint workflow for understanding metal–organic cage…

picks.title: Climate aridity amplifies global riverine nitrate beyond human inputs
picks.abstract: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Here we show, with machine-learning reconstructed global maps, that climate aridity is also a dominant driver, systematically elevating nitrate concentrations across land-use gradients and creating unexpected hotspots beyond major agricultural and urban centers. Across ~2.9 million river segments worldwide, nitrate concentrations exceed ecological and health thresholds across ~33 and 2% of global land area, affecting ~5.6 billion (73%) and 0.5 billion (6%) people, respectively. Ecological threshold exceedance occurs mostly in headwaters, and about half of the health threshold exceedance occurs in middle-income countries and sparsely populated landscapes. These findings cast nitrate pollution as an aridity-amplified risk, suggesting that aridification may increase nitrate exposure even without additional human inputs. They call for regulatory standards that reflect risks across broad concentration ranges.

picks.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
picks.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

picks.title: Atomic Layer Ordering of 2D van der Waals Ion Channels Enables Ultrathin and Highly Selective Membranes
picks.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
picks.abstract: Developing ultrathin, highly selective membranes that emulate biological ion channels is a primary goal of synthetic membrane technology. Although two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a promising platform for constructing subnanometer fluidic channels, simultaneously achieving high permeance and excellent selectivity in 2D ionic membranes remains a significant challenge. This bottleneck originates from the complexities involved in controlling the precise structural arrangement within nanosheet assemblies. In this work, we demonstrate that the atomic-layer ordering of 2D van der Waals (vdW) ion channels is a decisive factor in achieving ultrathin, highly selective membranes. By assembling 2D titania nanosheets with atomic layer-by-layer regularity, we fabricate atomic stacking membranes (ASMs) that achieve near-unity ion selectivity within an ultrathin (∼50 nm) framework. The structural regularity of these ASMs causes continuous overlap of the electrical double layer throughout the 2D ion channels, facilitating robust electrostatic regulation and maximizing selectivity. The result is further confirmed by transmission electron microscopy, grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations. Leveraging the “Lego-like” modular assembly advantage of ASMs, we demonstrate multifunctional heterostructural iontronic devices and gate-controlled iontronic transistors featuring on/off ratios up to 104. Furthermore, the well-ordered 2D ion channels within these ASMs enable high-performance osmotic energy harvesting. This solution-processable atomic-layer van der Waals assembly strategy for ultrathin and highly selective ASMs establishes a versatile platform for uniformly regulating 2D angstrom-scale ion transport, paving the way for advanced…

picks.title: Constructive Ordinal Exponentiation
picks.abstract: In classical mathematics, ordinal arithmetic is well-studied; constructively, addition and multiplication are well-known. We study constructive ordinal exponentiation, where ordinals are taken to be transitive, extensional, and wellfounded orders on sets. We present a negative result showing that general constructive ordinal exponentiation is impossible, but we suggest two definitions that come close. The first definition is abstract and solely motivated by the expected equations; this works as long as the base of the exponential is positive. The second definition is based on decreasing lists and can be seen as a constructive version of Sierpiński’s definition via functions with finite support; this requires the base to have a trichotomous least element. Whenever it makes sense to ask the question, the two constructions are equivalent, allowing us to prove algebraic laws, cancellation properties, and preservation of decidability of the exponential. The core ideas do not depend on any specific constructive set theory or type theory, but a concrete computer-checked mechanization using the Agda proof assistant is given in homotopy type theory.

picks.title: Hemodynamic spectral signatures across vigilance states: a whole-night EEG/fNIRS investigation
picks.abstract: Sleep is accompanied by coordinated changes in neuronal activity and cerebral hemodynamics. However, cortical hemodynamic signatures across sleep stages remain poorly characterized, partly because most human electroencephalography (EEG)/functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies are limited in duration, rarely capture deep or Rapid-Eye-Movement (REM) sleep, have low sampling rate, or rely on a sleep-deprivation paradigm, which limits the generalizability of findings. Here, we combined whole-night polysomnography, EEG and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) in healthy young adults, as a bedside technology to monitor cortical hemodynamic fluctuations. We recorded fNIRS using an optimal, personalized, locally dense bilateral frontoparietal montage, alongside peripheral physiology recordings (respiration, photoplethysmography, mean arterial pressure). We computed oscillatory components of oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin (HbO-HbR) spectra across sleep stages using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Additionally, we analyzed within the same regions an independent sleep EEG-fMRI dataset (no REM recorded). Our results are suggesting that across frontal and parietal regions, slow-frequency (0.002-0.1Hz) power increased during N1 sleep in HbO and then progressively attenuated across N2 and N3 sleep, in HbO, HbR, and fMRI. REM showed a re-emergence of very-low-frequency power (<0.01Hz) in HbO and HbR. Higher-frequency oscillations (0.15-0.5Hz; overlapping respiratory-band) were selectively enhanced during NREM sleep (largest increase during N3) and returned toward wake-like levels during REM in frontal regions, with regional differences. Peripheral signals captured systemic physiology oscillations but did not reproduce the cortical stage-specific patterns.…

more.title: Competing paramagnetic phases in the maple-leaf Heisenberg antiferromagnet
more.abstract: We establish a remarkably rich ground state phase diagram in the maple-leaf lattice spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet as a function of the three symmetry-inequivalent nearest-neighbor bonds using exact diagonalization and tower-of-states analysis on clusters up to N=36 sites. Besides a hexagonal plaquette state, a star-shaped valence bond solid state is discovered in close vicinity to the (canted) 120^° magnetic phase, strongly reminiscent of a de-confined critical point or Dirac spin liquid scenario on the triangular lattice antiferromagnets. Moreover, an exact dimer product-state is observed next to a collinear Néel-state, similar to the Shastry-Sutherland model. All identified phases compete in a parameter regime close to the isotropic point, providing a promising region for spin liquids to emerge. By analyzing Gutzwiller-projected wave-functions we identify a sliver of parameter regime where a gapped Z₂ spin liquid Ansatz is in astonishing agreement with the exact N=36 ground state. This rich competition of paramagnetic phases demonstrates that the maple-leaf antiferromagnet is a promising platform for exotic states of matter and quantum critical phenomena.

more.title: Infinite-order lattice chiral anomalies and C P T symmetry
more.abstract: A key property of a global symmetry's anomaly is its order: the smallest integer n for which the diagonal symmetry of the n-copy system is anomaly-free. While many familiar lattice anomalies have finite order, perturbative anomalies in the continuum-those captured by Feynman diagrams-have infinite order. In this paper, we show that the Onsager symmetry, a lattice realization of the chiral symmetry of a 1+1d massless Dirac fermion, has an order-two anomaly. However, imposing lattice CPT symmetry enhances this anomaly from order two to infinite order, yielding a lattice chiral symmetry structure that more faithfully matches the continuum chiral anomaly. We also discuss the corresponding 2+1d symmetry-protected topological phases for these infinite-order lattice anomalies.

more.title: NEFERTITI : Linking Early Galaxy Formation to the Assembly of the Milky Way
more.abstract: We use a new implementation of the NEFERTITI galaxy formation model, coupled to ∼30 high-resolution Caterpillar dark-matter simulations of Milky Way (MW) analogs, to connect early galaxy formation with the MW's assembly down to z = 0. Our locally constrained model resolves minihalos hosting the first Population III (Pop III) stars and self-consistently tracks inhomogeneous ionization and chemical enrichment. Pop III star formation begins at z ≃ 27, peaks at z ≃ 10–15, and persists down to z ≲ 5, producing Pop III systems with M * ∼ 10–5 × 10 5 M ⊙ . The present-day descendants of Pop III stars span [Fe/H] < −9 to ≈−1, with the most metal-poor stars typically enriched by a few (1–4) low-energy supernova progenitors. Pair-instability supernova descendants more commonly form in massive halos ( M vir > 10 8 M ⊙ ), often externally enriched, reflecting the strong feedback and delayed recovery following energetic explosions. These early systems serve as building blocks for the present-day Galaxy’s metal-poor component: although 90% of the total stellar mass formed in situ, the accreted component dominates at [Fe/H] < −1 and accounts for nearly all stars with [Fe/H] < −2.5. This accreted population is largely built by a few (∼5) massive ( M * > 10 8 M ⊙ ) destroyed dwarfs, but lower-mass systems become increasingly important at low metallicities, with ultrafaint and classical dwarf spheroidal analogs contributing ∼25% at [Fe/H] < −3. Our model simultaneously reproduces the properties of metal-poor MW stars and the JWST “Hebe” galaxy at z ∼ 11, supporting its identification as a pure Pop III system. Ultimately, NEFERTITI is a key tool to interpret upcoming local and high- z observations linking the near- and far-field cosmology.

more.title: Intrinsic disorder in the candidate quantum spin ice Pr 2 Zr 2 O 7
more.abstract: Quantum spin liquids with long-range entanglement are of great interest for applications in quantum technology. The quantum spin ice Pr₂Zr₂O₇ is a promising example, where it is believed that structural disorder plays a key role in enhancing quantum mechanical effects by introducing strains that split the ground state doublet akin to the effect of a local disordered transverse field. However, the precise defect structure responsible for this behaviour is unknown. Here we have determined the intrinsic defect structure of Pr₂Zr₂O₇ using neutron and x-ray scattering techniques supported by density functional theory. We find the main defect is the stuffing of Zr⁴⁺ sites by Pr³⁺ ions, accompanied by charge compensating O²⁻ vacancies, and the relaxation of a neighbouring O²⁻ ion to an interstitial site. Our results explain the single-ion magnetism by considering the non-magnetic singlets that arise on neighbouring sites as a result of the defect structure. These singlets account for additional features in the crystal electric field excitations. The effects caused by this low level of structural disorder are magnified since several neighbouring Pr sites are affected. This makes a significant contribution towards the observed broadening of pinch points in the magnetic diffuse scattering, which was previously attributed purely to quantum effects.

more.title: Near-Heisenberg-limited parallel amplitude estimation with logarithmic-depth circuits
more.abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation is one of the core subroutines in quantum algorithms. This paper gives a parallelized amplitude estimation (PAE) algorithm that simultaneously achieves near-Heisenberg scaling in the total number of queries and sub-linear scaling in the circuit depth, with respect to the estimation precision. The algorithm is composed of a global GHZ state followed by separated low-depth Grover circuits optimized by quantum signal processing techniques; the number of qubits in the GHZ state and the depth of each circuit is tunable as a trade-off way, which particularly enables even near-Heisenberg-limited and logarithmic-depth algorithm for amplitude estimation. We prove that this trade-off scaling is nearly optimal with use of the parallel quantum adversary method, against folklore on the impossibility of efficient parallelization in amplitude estimation. The proposed algorithm has a form of distributed quantum computing, which may be suitable for device implementation.

more.title: Ultraviolet and Optical Signatures of Late-time Disk Instabilities in Tidal Disruption Events
more.abstract: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) are unique probes of evolving accretion in supermassive black holes (BHs). Recent models of TDE disks show that they undergo brief thermal instabilities with temporal super-Eddington accretion at late times, which has been suggested as a possibility to explain the ubiquitous late radio emergence in TDEs. We model the ultraviolet (UV) and optical signatures of such disk instabilities, expected from the accretion power being reprocessed by the optically thick outflow following super-Eddington accretion. Our model predicts brief UV-bright transients lasting for days, with luminosities of 10 42 –10 43 erg s −1 in the near-UV and 10 41 –10 42 erg s −1 in the optical for a typical TDE by a 10 6 M ⊙ BH. These could be detectable by near-future surveys such as ULTRASAT, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and the Argus Array for TDEs at redshifts out to ≈0.1. We further conduct a search for these transients in existing nearby TDEs using data from the Zwicky Transient Facility, placing upper limits on the flare rate for each TDE of 1–2 yr −1 depending on the outflow mass. In the era of future surveys, combined UV/optical and radio monitoring would be an important test of the disk-instability phenomenon as well as its role in late-time radio emission in TDEs.

more.title: Characterizing the Scale Height and Filamentary Structure of Radiatively Cooled Magnetically Arrested Disks
more.abstract: Radiative cooling can strongly influence the structure and dynamics of black hole accretion disks. Here we perform general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations of magnetically arrested disks (MADs) around a nonspinning black hole. Radiative cooling is consistently included in the simulations, and its intensity is scaled by the mass accretion rate ranging from 10 − 7 M ̇ Edd to 1 0 − 4 M ̇ Edd . Considering synchrotron and bremsstrahlung emission, we quantify how radiative losses modify the disk structure and the accretion dynamics. In the inner MAD disk regions, accumulation of magnetic field regulates gas accretion, enforcing the gas into a discrete interchange-driven filamentary structure. We identify, both analytically and numerically, a transition mass accretion rate above which radiative cooling becomes faster than the heating, which is assumed to occur via local coupling to the magnetic field. Above this mass accretion rate, cooling substantially reduces the gas thermal pressure, leading to considerably thinner and denser accretion filaments and a substantial increase in radiative efficiency, relative to lower accretion rates. We show that under these conditions conventional measures of the disk scale height become misleading in MAD flows. We therefore introduce an alternative definition based on the polar position of the density maximum, which more robustly characterizes the filamentary structure of the disks in the presence of strong magnetic fields and cooling.

more.title: Stellar Population Spectra Incorporating Detailed Binary Evolution Using POSYDON
more.abstract: The accuracy of stellar population properties inferred through spectral energy distribution fitting hinges on the reliability of the underlying spectral models. Binary interactions are fundamental for massive star evolution, and ignoring their spectral contribution can lead to incorrect results. We use the POSYDON binary population synthesis code to generate spectral models of stellar populations that include binaries at solar metallicity. Our framework incorporates a collection of spectral libraries that is designed to address key outcomes of binary stellar evolution like wind-stripped Wolf–Rayet (WR) stars, binary-stripped helium (He) stars, and a treatment for stellar mergers. Our starburst spectral models confirm previous results showing that the inclusion of binary interactions has a significant effect on the ultraviolet (UV) and ionizing regime of the integrated spectrum. In particular we find that WR stars and other massive main-sequence stars dominate the production of ionizing radiation at earlier times, but after ≃16 Myr binary-stripped stars produced through mass transfer begin to dominate. Furthermore, we show that the production of ionizing He + photons is especially sensitive to the underlying population of binary-stripped stars. While our results currently focus on high-mass stars (≥4 M ⊙ ) at solar metallicity, they provide the framework for binary spectral synthesis across a range of metallicities and masses and lay the foundation for calculations of the emergent emission-line spectra in the UV, optical, and infrared regimes. We make the spectral models from this work publicly available for use in a format that can be integrated into fitting codes.

more.title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
more.abstract: Cannabis is the world's most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

more.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
more.abstract: RNA-derived 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1–3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2′,3′-cNMPs; 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3′→5′)-guanosine 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2′,3′-cAMP, 2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling. The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

more.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
more.abstract: Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1–3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program. A distinct physical nuclear state acquired by embryos at the beginning of life supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

more.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
more.abstract: Disconnects between in vitro and in vivo results in experimental biology have long been recognized as potential hurdles to understanding health and disease. A prototypical example of such a disconnect is the NLRP3 inflammasome, which mediates inflammation in diverse settings of disease and protective immunity1,2. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro requires two signals: (1) priming by pathogen-associated molecular patterns such as bacterial lipopolysaccharides and (2) activation by molecules that disrupt cellular homeostasis1,3. By contrast, the NLRP3 inflammasome in vivo is activated by lipopolysaccharide alone. The mechanisms that underlie the difference between in vitro and in vivo activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome are undefined. Here we report that extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness is a determinant of NLRP3 activities and that in vitro systems using physiological ECM stiffness enable one-signal in vivo-like NLRP3 activities to occur in human and mouse phagocytes. Physiological ECM stiffness induced expression of the transcription factor NRF2, which was found to be necessary for one-signal NLRP3 activation. Mechanistically, we identify Panx1 as an NRF2-regulated gene that promotes NLRP3 activity. Macrophages derived from the stiff matrix of the bone—osteoclasts—had reduced NRF2 levels and impaired NLRP3 activity. Moreover, alveolar macrophages from patients with pulmonary fibrosis displayed reduced NRF2 activity. Finally, NRF2 was required for antitumour immunity induced by cancer vaccines consisting of NLRP3 agonistic adjuvants. These findings indicate that NRF2 may be a transcriptional checkpoint that controls NLRP3 inflammasome activity. more.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
more.abstract: Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity 1–5 . We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells) 6 . Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1 ) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 ( Rgs2 ), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.

more.title: Seafloor geodesy delineates fast megathrust relocking after the giant 2011 Tohoku earthquake
more.abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.

more.title: Disrupting Hidden Antiaromaticity in N -Hydroxyphthalimide Reveals a Design Principle for Highly Reactive N -Oxyl Hydrogen Atom Transfer Mediators
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI) and its corresponding N-oxyl radical, phthalimide N-oxyl (PINO), have long been used as mediators for hydrogen atom transfer (HAT), particularly in radical-mediated C–H oxidations. Although numerous NHPI/PINO derivatives have been developed, the absence of an intuitive model connecting scaffold structure to intrinsic HAT reactivity has left catalyst development largely empirical. Herein, we show that insertion of a heteroatom between one carbonyl group of the NHPI/PINO framework and the fused aryl ring substantially accelerates HAT in electrochemically driven oxidations, with rate enhancements of up to 36-fold for benzylic alcohol substrates. This enhanced reactivity correlates with significantly larger computed O–H bond dissociation enthalpies relative to NHPI (ΔBDEO–H = 6.5–8.1 kcal/mol), which increase the thermodynamic driving force for HAT by the corresponding N-oxyl radicals. NICS, NBO, and DFT-based structural analyses support a model in which previously overlooked antiaromatic destabilization within the five-membered imide motif weakens the O–H bond of NHPI and is relieved upon formation of PINO. Among the heteroatom-containing analogues examined, sulfur-containing N-hydroxythiobenzouracil (NHTBU) provided a favorable balance of high HAT reactivity and catalyst persistence, enabling the electrochemical oxidation of numerous substrates under mild conditions with activity superior to NHPI.

more.title: Chemical Control of Quorum Sensing Rewires Mixed Bacterial Communities
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Microbial communities are central to host and environmental health, yet their dysregulation can drive diseases. Chemical strategies for selectively reprogramming community composition remain limited. Here, we show that agonists of the accessory gene regulator (agr) quorum sensing system provide a powerful, nonbactericidal approach to reshape staphylococcal biofilm communities. In mixed biofilms of multiple Staphylococcus epidermidis strains, selective agr activation produces pronounced sequence-dependent shifts in community composition in vitro. This targeted remodeling enhances the susceptibility of the community to antibiotic treatment. Extending this strategy to interspecies systems, we demonstrate that agr agonists reduce the abundance of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus by >95% in mixed biofilms with S. epidermidis without relying on bactericidal activity. Notably, the efficacy of agr-mediated community control is modulated by iron availability, revealing an environmental layer of regulation. Together, these findings support quorum sensing agonism as a chemically precise strategy to manipulate microbial communities by exploiting intrinsic signaling differences with implications spanning human health and agriculture.

more.title: Anti -Dihydroxylation-Enabled Dual-Resolution Profiling and Imaging of Fatty Acid C═C Bond Isomers
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Lipids are essential for membrane structure, signaling, and stress adaptation. Their diverse biological roles are largely dictated by the presence of C═C bonds in unsaturated fatty acids (FAs), which vary in both position and geometry. However, unambiguous characterization and in situ mapping of these two structural features have remained longstanding analytical challenges. Here, we present a stereochemistry-preserved chemical derivatization strategy coupled with trapped ion mobility spectrometry-tandem MS (TIMS-MS/MS), enabling complete resolution of both FA C═C bond position and geometry within a single workflow. This approach facilitates rapid and quantitative profiling of dynamic cis–trans isomerization in bacteria under diverse stress conditions and, notably, reveals a previously unrecognized dose-dependent antibiotic adaptation mechanism in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a multidrug-resistant pathogen. To translate this strategy to spatially resolved analyses, we developed an in situ derivatization workflow for mass spectrometry imaging, which uncovers the spatial heterogeneity of FA isomers in proximally cocultured, clinically relevant polymicrobial pathogens. These findings highlight colony-specific spatial dynamics of cis and trans lipid isomers and suggest lipid-mediated metabolic interactions between co-occurring microbial species. Together, this integrated platform enables both quantitative and spatial interrogation of lipid isomerization, providing new opportunities to systematically investigate its roles in microbial physiology, pathogenesis, and beyond.

more.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April–May 2026
more.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.

more.title: Structural and Electronic Properties of Lead Halide Perovskite Thin-Film Surfaces
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Polycrystalline perovskite thin films are consistently associated with high-performance optoelectronic devices. The main challenges currently under the spotlight lie with the stability and reliability of these devices, requiring a better understanding of thin-film surfaces and interfaces. However, their consistent investigation is often very challenging. Given the soft nature of these materials, there is a struggle to directly assign the origin of the electronic features and correlate them to the chemical nature of the surfaces. Here, by exploiting a multimodal approach, we measure, for the first time, at submicrometer scales, the diffraction patterns of the thin-film grain surface, which provide the material fingerprint and experimental evidence that the surface of such soft semiconductors is not as disordered as often claimed. Then, building on such knowledge, we move to ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy, which provides information about the electronic structure of the first few nanometers of the thin-film surface. Having identified the structural nature of the surface, we are eventually able to unambiguously assign the origin of the photoemission spectra for a wide range of metal halide perovskites. In particular, metallic lead is identified to be the origin of the often-reported midgap photoemissive states, thus far assigned to deep electronic states within the lead-halide perovskite semiconductor band gap. The chemical composition of the metal halides, the photodegradation of the perovskites under visible light, the quality of the precursors, and the actual stoichiometry of the thin film heavily define the presence of such states and elucidate the origin of carrier loss, photodegradation, and sample reproducibility in metal halide perovskite optoelectronics.

more.title: Label-free Raman spectroscopy for cancer therapy response: from methodological framework to clinical translation
more.abstract: The early detection of therapy-induced biomolecular changes and the prediction of therapeutic response remain major challenges in oncology. Current clinical methods often assess treatment response through macroscopic or morphological endpoints, whereas molecular alterations associated with sensitivity, resistance, or recurrence may arise earlier and remain undetected. Raman spectroscopy offers a label-free and non-destructive approach to probe the intrinsic biochemical composition of cells, tissues, and biofluids, providing spectral and spatial information that can support therapy response prediction and longitudinal monitoring. This review discusses Raman-based technologies for cancer therapy assessment, from preclinical models to emerging clinical applications. We first outline the clinical need for rapid, non-destructive, and molecularly informative tools, considering tumor heterogeneity, therapy resistance, the tumor microenvironment, and current standards for response evaluation. We then provide a methodological framework for selecting Raman modalities, including spontaneous Raman (SR) spectroscopy, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), stimulated Raman spectroscopy (SRS), and coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS), together with key considerations on acquisition strategies, multimodal integration, experimental design, preprocessing, feature analysis, and machine learning. We summarize Raman spectral biomarkers associated with therapy-induced changes in nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, metabolites, extracellular matrix components, and anticancer drugs, and critically examine studies using Raman spectroscopy to predict or monitor responses to major therapeutic approaches. more.title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
more.abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. more.title: Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation: From Prolapse to Precision Therapy
more.abstract: Degenerative mitral valve regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse affects ≈15 million people globally and is the commonest indication for mitral intervention in high-income countries, but its biology, natural history, and lifetime management are ill defined. This review summarizes current knowledge of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, risk stratification, and lifetime management of degenerative mitral regurgitation, with a focus on areas of uncertainty, recent advances, and emerging research directions. These include translational research focused on determining genetic and cellular drivers of disease progression and mechanistic studies geared to improve detection and prevention of downstream myocardial dysfunction, particularly in high-risk phenotypes, including arrhythmic mitral prolapse. The current landscape of randomized trials and large registries comparing contemporary surgical and transcatheter treatment and strategies to improve patient access to care and outcomes across all patient risk profiles and populations are also discussed.

more.title: Immersive Reality in Cardiothoracic Surgical Education
more.abstract: Immersive reality technologies, including virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, and related extended reality platforms, are reforming how surgeons learn complex anatomy, rehearse procedures, develop technical skills, and manage unexpected or rare intraoperative crises. Cardiothoracic surgery is particularly well suited to these tools because postgraduate training occurs in a high-stakes environment characterized by complex 3-dimensional anatomy, limited operative exposure, minimally invasive/robotic approaches, open communication, and the need for synchronized team performance. Immersive platforms facilitate anatomy education and procedural planning and enable deliberate practice and nontechnical skills training. Although most studies remain small, heterogeneous, and focused on surrogate outcomes rather than patient outcomes, evidence from surgical education and cardiothoracic surgery literature demonstrates that these tools impart improvement in knowledge, confidence, procedural accuracy, and simulator performance. This article defines immersive reality technologies, reviews their educational rationale and emerging applications in cardiothoracic surgery, proposes an implementation framework for training programs, and highlights limitations related to haptics, validation, privacy, equity, and regulatory oversight. The next phase should focus on validation of outcome-linked curricula that integrate immersive simulation into competency-based surgical education.

more.title: ANGPTL4 Inhibition in Adults with Elevated Triglyceride Levels
more.abstract: BACKGROUND: Angiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4) inhibits lipoprotein lipase and regulates triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism. MAR001 is a monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL4 that is being evaluated for lowering triglyceride levels. METHODS: We conducted a two-part, phase 2b, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. In part A, the focus of this report, we enrolled adults who had a nonfasting triglyceride level of at least 175 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 35 mg per deciliter at initial screening, followed by a fasting triglyceride level of at least 150 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 30 mg per deciliter on confirmatory screening. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to receive MAR001 at a dose of 300, 450, or 900 mg or matching placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 24 weeks. The primary end point was the percent change from baseline in the fasting triglyceride level at week 12, reported as the difference between each MAR001 dose group and the placebo group (placebo-adjusted change). RESULTS: A total of 236 participants were enrolled in the trial, with 177 assigned to receive MAR001 and 59 to receive placebo; a total of 235 participants received at least one dose of MAR001 or placebo and were included in the primary efficacy analyses. The mean age of the participants was 60.4 years, and 39% were women. The median triglyceride level at baseline was 249.5 mg per deciliter (interquartile range, 210.0 to 313.0). At week 12, in an intention-to-treat analysis, the placebo-adjusted least-squares mean percent changes in the fasting triglyceride level were -39.1 percentage points, -40.5 percentage points, and -45.3 percentage points for the 300-mg, 450-mg, and 900-mg doses,…

more.title: Surgical Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation
more.abstract: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart failure, mortality, and reduced quality of life. Although catheter ablation is the most widely used rhythm control strategy, its efficacy is limited in patients with non-paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and large left atria. To address this therapeutic gap, surgical approaches, including minimally invasive ablation, hybrid epicardial-endocardial strategies, and left atrial appendage exclusion, have continued to evolve. In this review, we focus on recent evidence to guide clinical decision-making on patient selection, advances in minimally invasive surgical and hybrid techniques, left atrial appendage exclusion, and postoperative anticoagulation management. Minimally invasive standalone Cox-Maze IV procedure and hybrid epicardial-endocardial ablation have demonstrated superior long-term freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmias compared with thoracoscopic epicardial surgical ablation or catheter ablation alone. Five-year arrhythmia-free survival has approached 85% to 95% in experienced centers after the Cox-Maze IV procedure and approximately 60% to 70% after hybrid ablation, compared with 35% to 45% after thoracoscopic epicardial ablation and 30% to 35% after single catheter ablation alone. Surgical left atrial appendage exclusion performed at the time of ablation may further reduce thromboembolic risk, although the optimal strategy for postprocedural anticoagulation remains uncertain. Careful patient selection remains essential, with atrial fibrillation type, duration, left atrial size, and previous treatment failure known to be key predictors of procedural success. more.title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for universality limits
more.abstract: We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for universality limits for orthogonal polynomials associated to a fixed measure on the real line and related systems. One of our results is that the Christoffel–Darboux kernel has sine kernel asymptotics at a point ξ ξ , with regularly varying scaling, if and only if the orthogonality measure (spectral measure) has a unique tangent measure at ξ ξ and that tangent measure is the Lebesgue measure. All previously known cases of sine kernel asymptotics, with absolutely continuous or singular measures, have regularly varying scaling. Our work is not limited to bulk universality; we show that the Christoffel–Darboux kernel has a regularly varying scaling limit with a nontrivial limit kernel if and only if the orthogonality measure has a unique tangent measure at ξ ξ and that tangent measure is not a point mass. The possible limit kernels correspond to homogeneous de Branges spaces; in particular, this equivalence completely characterizes several prominent universality classes such as hard edge universality, Fisher–Hartwig singularities, and jump discontinuities in the weights. A key ingredient in the proof is a new correspondence between measures and chains of de Branges spaces, not between Weyl functions and Hamiltonians. In order to handle limits with power law weights, this correspondence goes beyond the more common setting of Poisson-finite measures, and allows arbitrary power bounded measures.

more.title: Measuring spectral functions of doped magnets with Rydberg tweezer arrays
more.abstract: Spectroscopic measurements of single-particle spectral functions provide crucial insight into strongly correlated quantum matter by resolving the energy and spatial structure of elementary excitations. Here we introduce a spectroscopic protocol for single-charge injection with simultaneous spatial and energy resolution in a Rydberg tweezer array, effectively emulating scanning tunneling microscopy. By combining this protocol with single-atom–resolved imaging, we go beyond conventional spectroscopy by not only measuring the single-particle spectral function but also directly imaging the microscopic structure of the excitations underlying spectral resonances in frustrated tJ Hamiltonians in the kinetic limit (t>>J). We reveal resonances associated with the formation of bound magnetic polarons – composite quasiparticles consisting of a mobile hole bound to a magnon – and directly extract their binding energy, and image their spatial properties and spin character. Finally, by exploiting the spatial tunability of our platform, we measure the local density of states across different lattice geometries. Our work establishes Rydberg tweezer arrays as a powerful platform for spectroscopic studies of strongly correlated models, offering microscopic control and direct real-space access to emergent quasiparticles in engineered quantum matter.

more.title: Clumps in a Cocoon: Geometry and Mixing Set the Universal X-ray to Hα Surface Brightness Ratio
more.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
more.abstract: Recent observations reveal a nearly universal X-ray to Hα surface-brightness ratio, SBX/SBHα ~ 3, in galactic winds, ram-pressure-stripped tails, and cluster filaments. This is surprising, given the very different temperatures traced by the X-ray and Hα emission. Plane-parallel mixing-layer models do not recover this ratio. We run 3D wind-tunnel simulations in the high density-contrast (χ ~ 103) regime, where the cold phase shatters into small Hα-emitting clumps embedded in a volume-filling X-ray cocoon. After smoothing on the tail-width scale, the simulated ratio converges to the observed value. The hot-gas entrainment rate sets the bolometric luminosity, L_(bol) ∝ Mᵢₙ. Hα carries a nearly fixed fraction of this luminosity, set mainly by atomic emissivity near 104 K. The X-ray-emitting mass is the same entrainment rate multiplied by the residence time in the X-ray-emitting temperature band, and its luminosity is the corresponding thermal energy divided by the cooling time. Hence L_X∝ Mᵢₙ ∝ L_(bol), with the X-ray fraction set by the residence-to-cooling-time ratio. An age diagnostic constrains the residence time to be far shorter than the cooling time, making the X-ray and Hα fractions comparable. Their common scaling with Lbol explains the correlation, while the comparable bolometric fractions explain why the observed ratio is order unity.

more.abstract: The study of spontaneous symmetry breaking and electronic order is fundamental in condensed matter physics. Hidden order, symmetry-breaking states that elude conventional probes, potentially plays a crucial role in understanding complex quantum phases in a wide range of materials. Ferroaxial order, a state characterized by broken mirror symmetries while maintaining time-reversal and inversion symmetries, is one of the hidden orders that have proven most challenging to detect experimentally. Here, we demonstrate a new approach for investigating both the ferroaxial order parameter and ferroaxial susceptibility using elastoresistivity measurements. We do this for 1T-TiSe₂, a material that exhibits charge density wave order that has eluded comprehensive understanding for a long time. These measurements reveal an anomalous off-diagonal linear elastoresistivity in the CDW state. We discuss why this provides a smoking gun for ferroaxial order. Furthermore, we construct an appropriate combination of the symmetry-breaking strains ε_(x²-y²) and ε_(xy) that acts as an effective conjugate field for the ferroaxial order, and demonstrate how sweeping this effective field in the CDW state results in a hysteretic behavior of the elastoresistivity, associated with the movement of ferroaxial domain walls. Finally, we reveal a divergence of certain nonlinear elastoresistivity coefficients above the critical temperature, and discuss how this is consistent with a divergence of the ferroaxial susceptibility near T_ CDW  200K. Our study also includes detailed elastocaloric measurements, which reveal the presence of an additional phase transition several tens of Kelvin below T_ CDW. more.abstract: Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants.

However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors in cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B cell receptor multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which measures plasma cell clonality based on V gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. We demonstrate that BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V gene usage in cell culture and in mice with restricted or native plasma cell diversity. We then use BCR-MERFISH to elucidate the microbiota-dependent changes in plasma cell abundance, clonal diversity, and public clonotype usage in the mouse gut and the non-uniform distribution of plasma cell clones along the mouse ileum. Given that tissue context is an essential modulator of plasma cell dynamics, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may offer new insights into a wide range of immunological questions.

more.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference
more.abstract: When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

more.title: The Influence of Police Unions in Local Elections: Evidence from U.S. Cities’ Spending and Performance
more.abstract: Despite growing attention to local policies governing public safety issues, and mounting reports of police union spending to local candidates, the role of police unions in local politics remains understudied. We address this gap by assembling a novel, large-scale dataset on campaign finance in U.S. mayoral elections, covering 2,303 races across 1,073 cities from 2001 to 2019. We document that police unions frequently donate to mayoral candidates—especially in mid-sized and large cities—targeting likely winners and incumbents, and without displaying clear partisan bias. Using a within-city design that accounts for heterogeneous treatment effects in the presence of staggered treatment timing, we find that the election of a police-union-backed mayor leads to an expansion in police department size. However, we do not find improvements in police performance in these cities, suggesting that unions’ political involvement, while providing additional resources, might also be associated with reduced incentives for effort.

more.title: Kuroshio Extension warming shaped by Gulf Stream variability via the Arctic atmosphere
more.abstract: Recent unprecedented ocean warming has produced coherent sea surface temperature anomalies across the Northern Hemisphere extratropics. While the tropical Pacific is a natural source of North Pacific variability, the influence of the mid-latitude North Atlantic has remained poorly understood. Here we investigate whether Gulf Stream variability modulates Kuroshio Extension variability using 100-year idealized model simulations. We find that Gulf Stream variability remotely modulates Kuroshio Extension variability, explaining 13% of its internal sea surface temperature variance, whereas we find no evidence that Kuroshio variability similarly modulates the Gulf Stream. Positive Gulf Stream sea surface temperature anomalies excite a Northern Annular Mode-like atmospheric circulation response that weakens the Aleutian Low over the North Pacific. The resulting northward shift of the Kuroshio Extension enhances northward warm-water transport and promotes warming in the western mid-latitude North Pacific. We further show that a high-resolution ocean model is required to properly capture this coupling between Gulf Stream variability and atmospheric circulation, highlighting the importance of western boundary currents and associated oceanic fronts for this interbasin pathway. These findings indicate that North Atlantic variability contributed to the exceptional North Pacific warming during 2020–2024 and may provide a source of decadal predictability for Northern Hemisphere climate.

more.title: Accretion-powered flares from black hole–disc collisions in galactic nuclei
more.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
more.abstract: Black hole impacts on accretion discs in galactic nuclei can power luminous transients, but predicting their observable signatures is challenging because the post-collision flow is highly time-dependent and inhomogeneous. We present a radiative post-processing framework for relativistic hydrodynamics simulations of black hole–disc collisions. Using physically motivated prescriptions for shock heating, optical depth via an eikonal solver, and photon escape fractions that account for photon trapping and diffusion, we predict light curves and spectral energy distributions over a range of disc densities and collision velocities. Our results indicate that the emission is dominated by the long-lived accretion flow onto the secondary black hole, whose mass supply is highly super-Eddington, rather than by cooling of the unbound ejecta. In the parameter range explored, the luminosity is typically of the order of the Eddington luminosity of the secondary and can reach several times this value, and the emission is generically dominated by soft X-rays. We find that lower velocity collisions produce brighter flares, while the disc surface density mainly controls spectral evolution: low-density discs typically produce ∼keV-peaked flares with weak spectral evolution, whereas high-density discs show softer early emission and late-time hardening. A depletion-time estimate calibrated to our results suggests characteristic durations of hours to days for intermediate-mass secondaries, and yields tflare∝PQPE. We discuss implications for QPE-like transients and for the SMBH-binary candidate OJ 287. Our framework does not include radiative feedback on the gas, therefore the luminosities should be interpreted only as baseline estimates of the available power for radiation.

more.title: Fast, high-fidelity erasure detection of dual-rail qubits with symmetrically coupled readout
more.abstract: Erasure qubits are a promising platform for implementing hardware-efficient quantum error correction. Realizing the error-correction advantages of this encoding requires frequent mid-circuit erasure checks that are fast, high-fidelity, and scalable. Here, we realize erasure detection with a hardware-efficient circuit consisting of a single readout resonator dispersively and symmetrically coupled to both transmons of a dual-rail qubit. We use this circuit to demonstrate single-shot erasure detection in 384 ns with minimal impact on the dual-rail logical manifold, achieving a residual error per check of 6.0(2) × 10⁻⁴, with only 8(3) × 10⁻⁵ induced dephasing per check, and an erasure error per check of 2.54(1)× 10⁻². The high degree of matched dispersive readout coupling (χ-matching) within the dual-rail qubit code space also allows us to realize a new modality: time-continuous erasure detection performed in parallel with single-qubit gates. Here we achieve a median 7.2 × 10⁻⁵ error per gate with < 1 × 10⁻⁵ error induced by erasure detection. This demonstrates a reduction in erasure detection overhead as well as a crucial ingredient for soft information quantum error correction. Together, these results establish symmetrically coupled dispersive readout as a fast, hardware-efficient, and scalable component for erasure-based quantum error correction using transmon dual-rail qubits.

shortlist.title: UNCOVER/MegaScience Finds Uniform and Highly Bursty Star Formation at 3 < z < 9, Consistent with the High-redshift UV Luminosity Function
shortlist.abstract: Star formation timescales are key to understanding fundamental physics like feedback mechanisms, as well as the abundance of bright galaxies at z > 10. We investigate galaxy star formation histories (SFHs) and their evolution across z ∼ 3–9 by measuring the line-to-UV ratio ( R line ) and line equivalent width (EW) of H α +[N ii ] and [O iii ]+H β directly from UNCOVER/MegaScience spectro-photometry without relying on a specific SFH or nebular line modeling. Our photometric measurements recover R line and EW to <10% systematic accuracy compared to spectroscopy. This allows us to construct a large mass- (and flux-) complete sample and quantitatively examine how R line evolves with redshift and stellar mass. We find that the intrinsic scatter in R line does not significantly evolve with redshift across 3 < z < 7, though it may increase at z ≳ 8. We build population-level toy models using fsps to help interpret our observations, and find that scatter in R line primarily reflects the amplitude of SFH fluctuations; this implies that our observed lack of evolution in the scatter of R line is due to similar star formation burstiness from z ∼ 3 to z ∼ 7. Our observations are best reproduced by a set of SFHs with rising, long-duration, and large-amplitude bursts. Finally, we demonstrate that the toy model that best describes our z ∼ 6 data can boost UV brightness by up to Δ M UV ∼ −2.0 mag compared with a 200 Myr constant SFH, and naturally produces a large number of galaxies at z > 10. This suggests that no significant evolution in star formation burstiness is required to explain the abundance of UV-bright galaxies at high redshift.

shortlist.title: Trapping 11 thousand atoms in a tweezer array generated by a single metasurface
shortlist.abstract: The scalability of physical qubit numbers is a central challenge toward a universal fault-tolerant quantum computer. Here, we robustly trap 11,000 individual atoms in a tweezer array, thereby enabling the available single atom resource above the 10,000-atom level for the first time in neutral atom quantum computation platforms. This advance is enabled by a single metasurface, approximately 2 cm in diameter, that generates the entire tweezer array without the need for microscope objectives, thereby maximizing laser-power efficiency. The large aperture ensures a working distance of about 1.5 cm, allowing the metasurface to be placed outside the vacuum cell and avoiding the technical complications of in-vacuum operation. We further characterize the randomly loaded atom array using the statistical theory of percolation phase transitions. This work takes an important first step toward a quantum computer at the 10,000-qubit scale.

shortlist.title: Statistical characterization of valley coupling in Si/SiGe quantum dots via g -factor measurements near a valley vortex
shortlist.abstract: The presence of low-energy valley excitations in Si/SiGe heterostructures often causes spin qubits to fail. It is therefore important to develop robust protocols for characterizing the valley coupling. Here, we show that realistically sized samplings of valley energy distributions tend to dramatically overestimate the average valley coupling. But we find that knowledge of the valley phase, in addition to the valley splitting, can significantly improve our estimates. Motivated by this understanding, we propose a novel method to probe the valley phase landscape across the quantum well using simple g-factor measurements. An important calibration step in this procedure is to measure g in a loop enclosing a valley vortex, where the valley phase winds by 2 π around a zero of the valley splitting. This proposal establishes an important new tool for probing spin qubits, and it can be implemented in current experiments.

shortlist.title: Competing paramagnetic phases in the maple-leaf Heisenberg antiferromagnet
shortlist.abstract: We establish a remarkably rich ground state phase diagram in the maple-leaf lattice spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet as a function of the three symmetry-inequivalent nearest-neighbor bonds using exact diagonalization and tower-of-states analysis on clusters up to N=36 sites. Besides a hexagonal plaquette state, a star-shaped valence bond solid state is discovered in close vicinity to the (canted) 120^° magnetic phase, strongly reminiscent of a de-confined critical point or Dirac spin liquid scenario on the triangular lattice antiferromagnets. Moreover, an exact dimer product-state is observed next to a collinear Néel-state, similar to the Shastry-Sutherland model. All identified phases compete in a parameter regime close to the isotropic point, providing a promising region for spin liquids to emerge. By analyzing Gutzwiller-projected wave-functions we identify a sliver of parameter regime where a gapped Z₂ spin liquid Ansatz is in astonishing agreement with the exact N=36 ground state. This rich competition of paramagnetic phases demonstrates that the maple-leaf antiferromagnet is a promising platform for exotic states of matter and quantum critical phenomena.

shortlist.title: Mean-motion Resonances in the Accretion Disks of Active Galactic Nuclei
shortlist.abstract: Mean-motion resonances (MMRs) are a generic outcome of convergent migration for bodies embedded in accretion disks around a central mass. Long studied in planetary systems, the same phenomenon should occur for stellar-mass black holes (BHs) in the disks of active galactic nuclei (AGN). In this work, we derive simple analytic criteria describing when BH pairs are driven out of resonance, and use them to chart MMR stability across AGN parameter space, accounting for disruption from general-relativistic apsidal precession, hydrodynamic turbulence, and stellar stirring. Across plausible AGN disk models, we find three MBH mass regimes: (i) for M / M ⊙ ≳ 10 7.5 , first-order resonances are generically unstable; (ii) for M / M ⊙ ≲ 10 6.5 , stable MMRs are always present; and (iii) for 10 6.5 ≲ M / M ⊙ ≲ 10 7.5 , stability depends on disk mass flux, the summed mass of the orbiters, and the nuclear-cusp slope. When present, stable MMRs commonly occur between an inner anti-trap and an outer trap set by thermal torques, a region where embedded objects migrate outward in the disk. These results imply that high-mass AGN allow convergent migration to proceed to LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK)-band mergers largely without resonant chains, whereas low- and intermediate-mass AGN can host MMRs, with the potential to reshape merger pathways.

shortlist.title: Infinite-order lattice chiral anomalies and C P T symmetry
shortlist.abstract: A key property of a global symmetry's anomaly is its order: the smallest integer n for which the diagonal symmetry of the n-copy system is anomaly-free. While many familiar lattice anomalies have finite order, perturbative anomalies in the continuum-those captured by Feynman diagrams-have infinite order. In this paper, we show that the Onsager symmetry, a lattice realization of the chiral symmetry of a 1+1d massless Dirac fermion, has an order-two anomaly. However, imposing lattice CPT symmetry enhances this anomaly from order two to infinite order, yielding a lattice chiral symmetry structure that more faithfully matches the continuum chiral anomaly. We also discuss the corresponding 2+1d symmetry-protected topological phases for these infinite-order lattice anomalies.

shortlist.title: NEFERTITI : Linking Early Galaxy Formation to the Assembly of the Milky Way
shortlist.abstract: We use a new implementation of the NEFERTITI galaxy formation model, coupled to ∼30 high-resolution Caterpillar dark-matter simulations of Milky Way (MW) analogs, to connect early galaxy formation with the MW's assembly down to z = 0. Our locally constrained model resolves minihalos hosting the first Population III (Pop III) stars and self-consistently tracks inhomogeneous ionization and chemical enrichment. Pop III star formation begins at z ≃ 27, peaks at z ≃ 10–15, and persists down to z ≲ 5, producing Pop III systems with M * ∼ 10–5 × 10 5 M ⊙ . The present-day descendants of Pop III stars span [Fe/H] < −9 to ≈−1, with the most metal-poor stars typically enriched by a few (1–4) low-energy supernova progenitors. Pair-instability supernova descendants more commonly form in massive halos ( M vir > 10 8 M ⊙ ), often externally enriched, reflecting the strong feedback and delayed recovery following energetic explosions. These early systems serve as building blocks for the present-day Galaxy’s metal-poor component: although 90% of the total stellar mass formed in situ, the accreted component dominates at [Fe/H] < −1 and accounts for nearly all stars with [Fe/H] < −2.5. This accreted population is largely built by a few (∼5) massive ( M * > 10 8 M ⊙ ) destroyed dwarfs, but lower-mass systems become increasingly important at low metallicities, with ultrafaint and classical dwarf spheroidal analogs contributing ∼25% at [Fe/H] < −3. Our model simultaneously reproduces the properties of metal-poor MW stars and the JWST “Hebe” galaxy at z ∼ 11, supporting its identification as a pure Pop III system. Ultimately, NEFERTITI is a key tool to interpret upcoming local and high- z observations linking the near- and far-field cosmology.
