shortlist.title: Expanding Chemical Space Enables Data–Driven Structure–Activity Relationships in Cage Catalysis
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Data-driven approaches are increasingly popular in catalysis, supplementing and even replacing traditional strategies that relied on empirical optimization. However, their application in the field of bioinspired cage catalysis remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the limited chemical space of known catalytically active cages. As a result, mechanistic insights are often obtained using computationally intensive DFT calculations on a handful of structurally similar cages. As chemical systems grow in complexity, this approach becomes impractical. Herein, we report a framework that significantly expedites the exploration of a much wider structural landscape while offering computational insights. This is made possible by a novel in situ experimental procedure─which circumvents the traditional time-consuming process of prepare, isolate, characterize, and test─coupled with data-driven methods to identify molecular features that govern activity. Using this approach, we experimentally explore 30 unique PdnL2n cages (n = 2–4) that mediate a nitro-aldol reaction with activities spanning over 4 orders of magnitude. Using this data set, a random forest model trained on molecular descriptors was developed to predict ΔG‡ (MAE of 0.4 kcal mol–1 and R2 = 0.9). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis highlighted geometric preorganization and electrostatic interactions within the cage as key determinants of catalytic efficiency. Moreover, DFT calculations on a selection of cages further validated these insights, indicating that meaningful mechanistic understanding can be achieved at significantly reduced computational cost. We anticipate that this integrated, screening, data-driven, mechanistic strategy will provide a blueprint workflow for understanding metal–organic cage…

shortlist.title: Ultraviolet and Optical Signatures of Late-time Disk Instabilities in Tidal Disruption Events
shortlist.abstract: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) are unique probes of evolving accretion in supermassive black holes (BHs). Recent models of TDE disks show that they undergo brief thermal instabilities with temporal super-Eddington accretion at late times, which has been suggested as a possibility to explain the ubiquitous late radio emergence in TDEs. We model the ultraviolet (UV) and optical signatures of such disk instabilities, expected from the accretion power being reprocessed by the optically thick outflow following super-Eddington accretion. Our model predicts brief UV-bright transients lasting for days, with luminosities of 10 42 –10 43 erg s −1 in the near-UV and 10 41 –10 42 erg s −1 in the optical for a typical TDE by a 10 6 M ⊙ BH. These could be detectable by near-future surveys such as ULTRASAT, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and the Argus Array for TDEs at redshifts out to ≈0.1. We further conduct a search for these transients in existing nearby TDEs using data from the Zwicky Transient Facility, placing upper limits on the flare rate for each TDE of 1–2 yr −1 depending on the outflow mass. In the era of future surveys, combined UV/optical and radio monitoring would be an important test of the disk-instability phenomenon as well as its role in late-time radio emission in TDEs.

shortlist.title: Climate aridity amplifies global riverine nitrate beyond human inputs
shortlist.abstract: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Here we show, with machine-learning reconstructed global maps, that climate aridity is also a dominant driver, systematically elevating nitrate concentrations across land-use gradients and creating unexpected hotspots beyond major agricultural and urban centers. Across ~2.9 million river segments worldwide, nitrate concentrations exceed ecological and health thresholds across ~33 and 2% of global land area, affecting ~5.6 billion (73%) and 0.5 billion (6%) people, respectively. Ecological threshold exceedance occurs mostly in headwaters, and about half of the health threshold exceedance occurs in middle-income countries and sparsely populated landscapes. These findings cast nitrate pollution as an aridity-amplified risk, suggesting that aridification may increase nitrate exposure even without additional human inputs. They call for regulatory standards that reflect risks across broad concentration ranges.

shortlist.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
shortlist.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

shortlist.title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
shortlist.abstract: Cannabis is the world's most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

shortlist.title: Atomic Layer Ordering of 2D van der Waals Ion Channels Enables Ultrathin and Highly Selective Membranes
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Developing ultrathin, highly selective membranes that emulate biological ion channels is a primary goal of synthetic membrane technology. Although two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a promising platform for constructing subnanometer fluidic channels, simultaneously achieving high permeance and excellent selectivity in 2D ionic membranes remains a significant challenge. This bottleneck originates from the complexities involved in controlling the precise structural arrangement within nanosheet assemblies. In this work, we demonstrate that the atomic-layer ordering of 2D van der Waals (vdW) ion channels is a decisive factor in achieving ultrathin, highly selective membranes. By assembling 2D titania nanosheets with atomic layer-by-layer regularity, we fabricate atomic stacking membranes (ASMs) that achieve near-unity ion selectivity within an ultrathin (∼50 nm) framework. The structural regularity of these ASMs causes continuous overlap of the electrical double layer throughout the 2D ion channels, facilitating robust electrostatic regulation and maximizing selectivity. The result is further confirmed by transmission electron microscopy, grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations. Leveraging the “Lego-like” modular assembly advantage of ASMs, we demonstrate multifunctional heterostructural iontronic devices and gate-controlled iontronic transistors featuring on/off ratios up to 104. Furthermore, the well-ordered 2D ion channels within these ASMs enable high-performance osmotic energy harvesting. This solution-processable atomic-layer van der Waals assembly strategy for ultrathin and highly selective ASMs establishes a versatile platform for uniformly regulating 2D angstrom-scale ion transport, paving the way for advanced…

shortlist.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
shortlist.abstract: RNA-derived 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1–3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2′,3′-cNMPs; 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3′→5′)-guanosine 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2′,3′-cAMP, 2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling. The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

shortlist.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
shortlist.abstract: Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1–3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program. shortlist.abstract: Disconnects between in vitro and in vivo results in experimental biology have long been recognized as potential hurdles to understanding health and disease. A prototypical example of such a disconnect is the NLRP3 inflammasome, which mediates inflammation in diverse settings of disease and protective immunity1,2. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro requires two signals: (1) priming by pathogen-associated molecular patterns such as bacterial lipopolysaccharides and (2) activation by molecules that disrupt cellular homeostasis1,3. By contrast, the NLRP3 inflammasome in vivo is activated by lipopolysaccharide alone. The mechanisms that underlie the difference between in vitro and in vivo activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome are undefined. Here we report that extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness is a determinant of NLRP3 activities and that in vitro systems using physiological ECM stiffness enable one-signal in vivo-like NLRP3 activities to occur in human and mouse phagocytes. Physiological ECM stiffness induced expression of the transcription factor NRF2, which was found to be necessary for one-signal NLRP3 activation. Mechanistically, we identify Panx1 as an NRF2-regulated gene that promotes NLRP3 activity. Macrophages derived from the stiff matrix of the bone—osteoclasts—had reduced NRF2 levels and impaired NLRP3 activity. Moreover, alveolar macrophages from patients with pulmonary fibrosis displayed reduced NRF2 activity. Finally, NRF2 was required for antitumour immunity induced by cancer vaccines consisting of NLRP3 agonistic adjuvants. These findings indicate that NRF2 may be a transcriptional checkpoint that controls NLRP3 inflammasome activity. shortlist.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
shortlist.abstract: Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity 1–5 . We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells) 6 . Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1 ) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 ( Rgs2 ), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.

shortlist.title: Constructive Ordinal Exponentiation
shortlist.abstract: In classical mathematics, ordinal arithmetic is well-studied; constructively, addition and multiplication are well-known. We study constructive ordinal exponentiation, where ordinals are taken to be transitive, extensional, and wellfounded orders on sets. We present a negative result showing that general constructive ordinal exponentiation is impossible, but we suggest two definitions that come close. The first definition is abstract and solely motivated by the expected equations; this works as long as the base of the exponential is positive. The second definition is based on decreasing lists and can be seen as a constructive version of Sierpiński’s definition via functions with finite support; this requires the base to have a trichotomous least element. Whenever it makes sense to ask the question, the two constructions are equivalent, allowing us to prove algebraic laws, cancellation properties, and preservation of decidability of the exponential. The core ideas do not depend on any specific constructive set theory or type theory, but a concrete computer-checked mechanization using the Agda proof assistant is given in homotopy type theory.

shortlist.title: Disrupting Hidden Antiaromaticity in N -Hydroxyphthalimide Reveals a Design Principle for Highly Reactive N -Oxyl Hydrogen Atom Transfer Mediators
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI) and its corresponding N-oxyl radical, phthalimide N-oxyl (PINO), have long been used as mediators for hydrogen atom transfer (HAT), particularly in radical-mediated C–H oxidations. Although numerous NHPI/PINO derivatives have been developed, the absence of an intuitive model connecting scaffold structure to intrinsic HAT reactivity has left catalyst development largely empirical. Herein, we show that insertion of a heteroatom between one carbonyl group of the NHPI/PINO framework and the fused aryl ring substantially accelerates HAT in electrochemically driven oxidations, with rate enhancements of up to 36-fold for benzylic alcohol substrates. This enhanced reactivity correlates with significantly larger computed O–H bond dissociation enthalpies relative to NHPI (ΔBDEO–H = 6.5–8.1 kcal/mol), which increase the thermodynamic driving force for HAT by the corresponding N-oxyl radicals. NICS, NBO, and DFT-based structural analyses support a model in which previously overlooked antiaromatic destabilization within the five-membered imide motif weakens the O–H bond of NHPI and is relieved upon formation of PINO. Among the heteroatom-containing analogues examined, sulfur-containing N-hydroxythiobenzouracil (NHTBU) provided a favorable balance of high HAT reactivity and catalyst persistence, enabling the electrochemical oxidation of numerous substrates under mild conditions with activity superior to NHPI.

shortlist.title: Chemical Control of Quorum Sensing Rewires Mixed Bacterial Communities
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Microbial communities are central to host and environmental health, yet their dysregulation can drive diseases. Chemical strategies for selectively reprogramming community composition remain limited. Here, we show that agonists of the accessory gene regulator (agr) quorum sensing system provide a powerful, nonbactericidal approach to reshape staphylococcal biofilm communities. In mixed biofilms of multiple Staphylococcus epidermidis strains, selective agr activation produces pronounced sequence-dependent shifts in community composition in vitro. This targeted remodeling enhances the susceptibility of the community to antibiotic treatment. Extending this strategy to interspecies systems, we demonstrate that agr agonists reduce the abundance of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus by >95% in mixed biofilms with S. epidermidis without relying on bactericidal activity. Notably, the efficacy of agr-mediated community control is modulated by iron availability, revealing an environmental layer of regulation. Together, these findings support quorum sensing agonism as a chemically precise strategy to manipulate microbial communities by exploiting intrinsic signaling differences with implications spanning human health and agriculture.

shortlist.title: Label-free Raman spectroscopy for cancer therapy response: from methodological framework to clinical translation
shortlist.abstract: The early detection of therapy-induced biomolecular changes and the prediction of therapeutic response remain major challenges in oncology. Current clinical methods often assess treatment response through macroscopic or morphological endpoints, whereas molecular alterations associated with sensitivity, resistance, or recurrence may arise earlier and remain undetected. Raman spectroscopy offers a label-free and non-destructive approach to probe the intrinsic biochemical composition of cells, tissues, and biofluids, providing spectral and spatial information that can support therapy response prediction and longitudinal monitoring. This review discusses Raman-based technologies for cancer therapy assessment, from preclinical models to emerging clinical applications. We first outline the clinical need for rapid, non-destructive, and molecularly informative tools, considering tumor heterogeneity, therapy resistance, the tumor microenvironment, and current standards for response evaluation. We then provide a methodological framework for selecting Raman modalities, including spontaneous Raman (SR) spectroscopy, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), stimulated Raman spectroscopy (SRS), and coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS), together with key considerations on acquisition strategies, multimodal integration, experimental design, preprocessing, feature analysis, and machine learning. We summarize Raman spectral biomarkers associated with therapy-induced changes in nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, metabolites, extracellular matrix components, and anticancer drugs, and critically examine studies using Raman spectroscopy to predict or monitor responses to major therapeutic approaches. shortlist.title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
shortlist.abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. shortlist.title: Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation: From Prolapse to Precision Therapy
shortlist.abstract: Degenerative mitral valve regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse affects ≈15 million people globally and is the commonest indication for mitral intervention in high-income countries, but its biology, natural history, and lifetime management are ill defined. This review summarizes current knowledge of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, risk stratification, and lifetime management of degenerative mitral regurgitation, with a focus on areas of uncertainty, recent advances, and emerging research directions. These include translational research focused on determining genetic and cellular drivers of disease progression and mechanistic studies geared to improve detection and prevention of downstream myocardial dysfunction, particularly in high-risk phenotypes, including arrhythmic mitral prolapse. The current landscape of randomized trials and large registries comparing contemporary surgical and transcatheter treatment and strategies to improve patient access to care and outcomes across all patient risk profiles and populations are also discussed.

shortlist.title: Immersive Reality in Cardiothoracic Surgical Education
shortlist.abstract: Immersive reality technologies, including virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, and related extended reality platforms, are reforming how surgeons learn complex anatomy, rehearse procedures, develop technical skills, and manage unexpected or rare intraoperative crises. Cardiothoracic surgery is particularly well suited to these tools because postgraduate training occurs in a high-stakes environment characterized by complex 3-dimensional anatomy, limited operative exposure, minimally invasive/robotic approaches, open communication, and the need for synchronized team performance. Immersive platforms facilitate anatomy education and procedural planning and enable deliberate practice and nontechnical skills training. Although most studies remain small, heterogeneous, and focused on surrogate outcomes rather than patient outcomes, evidence from surgical education and cardiothoracic surgery literature demonstrates that these tools impart improvement in knowledge, confidence, procedural accuracy, and simulator performance. This article defines immersive reality technologies, reviews their educational rationale and emerging applications in cardiothoracic surgery, proposes an implementation framework for training programs, and highlights limitations related to haptics, validation, privacy, equity, and regulatory oversight. The next phase should focus on validation of outcome-linked curricula that integrate immersive simulation into competency-based surgical education.

shortlist.abstract: BACKGROUND: Angiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4) inhibits lipoprotein lipase and regulates triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism. MAR001 is a monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL4 that is being evaluated for lowering triglyceride levels. METHODS: We conducted a two-part, phase 2b, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. In part A, the focus of this report, we enrolled adults who had a nonfasting triglyceride level of at least 175 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 35 mg per deciliter at initial screening, followed by a fasting triglyceride level of at least 150 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 30 mg per deciliter on confirmatory screening. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to receive MAR001 at a dose of 300, 450, or 900 mg or matching placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 24 weeks. The primary end point was the percent change from baseline in the fasting triglyceride level at week 12, reported as the difference between each MAR001 dose group and the placebo group (placebo-adjusted change). RESULTS: A total of 236 participants were enrolled in the trial, with 177 assigned to receive MAR001 and 59 to receive placebo; a total of 235 participants received at least one dose of MAR001 or placebo and were included in the primary efficacy analyses. The mean age of the participants was 60.4 years, and 39% were women. The median triglyceride level at baseline was 249.5 mg per deciliter (interquartile range, 210.0 to 313.0). shortlist.title: Surgical Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation
shortlist.abstract: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart failure, mortality, and reduced quality of life. Although catheter ablation is the most widely used rhythm control strategy, its efficacy is limited in patients with non-paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and large left atria. To address this therapeutic gap, surgical approaches, including minimally invasive ablation, hybrid epicardial-endocardial strategies, and left atrial appendage exclusion, have continued to evolve. In this review, we focus on recent evidence to guide clinical decision-making on patient selection, advances in minimally invasive surgical and hybrid techniques, left atrial appendage exclusion, and postoperative anticoagulation management. Minimally invasive standalone Cox-Maze IV procedure and hybrid epicardial-endocardial ablation have demonstrated superior long-term freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmias compared with thoracoscopic epicardial surgical ablation or catheter ablation alone. Five-year arrhythmia-free survival has approached 85% to 95% in experienced centers after the Cox-Maze IV procedure and approximately 60% to 70% after hybrid ablation, compared with 35% to 45% after thoracoscopic epicardial ablation and 30% to 35% after single catheter ablation alone. Surgical left atrial appendage exclusion performed at the time of ablation may further reduce thromboembolic risk, although the optimal strategy for postprocedural anticoagulation remains uncertain. Careful patient selection remains essential, with atrial fibrillation type, duration, left atrial size, and previous treatment failure known to be key predictors of procedural success. shortlist.title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for universality limits
shortlist.abstract: We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for universality limits for orthogonal polynomials associated to a fixed measure on the real line and related systems. One of our results is that the Christoffel–Darboux kernel has sine kernel asymptotics at a point ξ ξ , with regularly varying scaling, if and only if the orthogonality measure (spectral measure) has a unique tangent measure at ξ ξ and that tangent measure is the Lebesgue measure. All previously known cases of sine kernel asymptotics, with absolutely continuous or singular measures, have regularly varying scaling. Our work is not limited to bulk universality; we show that the Christoffel–Darboux kernel has a regularly varying scaling limit with a nontrivial limit kernel if and only if the orthogonality measure has a unique tangent measure at ξ ξ and that tangent measure is not a point mass. The possible limit kernels correspond to homogeneous de Branges spaces; in particular, this equivalence completely characterizes several prominent universality classes such as hard edge universality, Fisher–Hartwig singularities, and jump discontinuities in the weights. A key ingredient in the proof is a new correspondence between measures and chains of de Branges spaces, not between Weyl functions and Hamiltonians. In order to handle limits with power law weights, this correspondence goes beyond the more common setting of Poisson-finite measures, and allows arbitrary power bounded measures.

shortlist.title: Measuring spectral functions of doped magnets with Rydberg tweezer arrays
shortlist.abstract: Spectroscopic measurements of single-particle spectral functions provide crucial insight into strongly correlated quantum matter by resolving the energy and spatial structure of elementary excitations. Here we introduce a spectroscopic protocol for single-charge injection with simultaneous spatial and energy resolution in a Rydberg tweezer array, effectively emulating scanning tunneling microscopy. By combining this protocol with single-atom–resolved imaging, we go beyond conventional spectroscopy by not only measuring the single-particle spectral function but also directly imaging the microscopic structure of the excitations underlying spectral resonances in frustrated tJ Hamiltonians in the kinetic limit (t>>J). We reveal resonances associated with the formation of bound magnetic polarons – composite quasiparticles consisting of a mobile hole bound to a magnon – and directly extract their binding energy, and image their spatial properties and spin character. Finally, by exploiting the spatial tunability of our platform, we measure the local density of states across different lattice geometries. Our work establishes Rydberg tweezer arrays as a powerful platform for spectroscopic studies of strongly correlated models, offering microscopic control and direct real-space access to emergent quasiparticles in engineered quantum matter.

shortlist.title: Clumps in a Cocoon: Geometry and Mixing Set the Universal X-ray to Hα Surface Brightness Ratio
shortlist.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
shortlist.abstract: Recent observations reveal a nearly universal X-ray to Hα surface-brightness ratio, SBX/SBHα ~ 3, in galactic winds, ram-pressure-stripped tails, and cluster filaments. This is surprising, given the very different temperatures traced by the X-ray and Hα emission. Plane-parallel mixing-layer models do not recover this ratio. We run 3D wind-tunnel simulations in the high density-contrast (χ ~ 103) regime, where the cold phase shatters into small Hα-emitting clumps embedded in a volume-filling X-ray cocoon. After smoothing on the tail-width scale, the simulated ratio converges to the observed value. The hot-gas entrainment rate sets the bolometric luminosity, L_(bol) ∝ Mᵢₙ. Hα carries a nearly fixed fraction of this luminosity, set mainly by atomic emissivity near 104 K. The X-ray-emitting mass is the same entrainment rate multiplied by the residence time in the X-ray-emitting temperature band, and its luminosity is the corresponding thermal energy divided by the cooling time. Hence L_X∝ Mᵢₙ ∝ L_(bol), with the X-ray fraction set by the residence-to-cooling-time ratio. An age diagnostic constrains the residence time to be far shorter than the cooling time, making the X-ray and Hα fractions comparable. Their common scaling with Lbol explains the correlation, while the comparable bolometric fractions explain why the observed ratio is order unity.

shortlist.abstract: The study of spontaneous symmetry breaking and electronic order is fundamental in condensed matter physics. Hidden order, symmetry-breaking states that elude conventional probes, potentially plays a crucial role in understanding complex quantum phases in a wide range of materials. Ferroaxial order, a state characterized by broken mirror symmetries while maintaining time-reversal and inversion symmetries, is one of the hidden orders that have proven most challenging to detect experimentally. Here, we demonstrate a new approach for investigating both the ferroaxial order parameter and ferroaxial susceptibility using elastoresistivity measurements. We do this for 1T-TiSe₂, a material that exhibits charge density wave order that has eluded comprehensive understanding for a long time. shortlist.abstract: Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants.

However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors in cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B cell receptor multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which measures plasma cell clonality based on V gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. shortlist.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference
shortlist.abstract: When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

shortlist.title: The Influence of Police Unions in Local Elections: Evidence from U.S. Cities’ Spending and Performance
shortlist.abstract: Despite growing attention to local policies governing public safety issues, and mounting reports of police union spending to local candidates, the role of police unions in local politics remains understudied. We address this gap by assembling a novel, large-scale dataset on campaign finance in U.S. mayoral elections, covering 2,303 races across 1,073 cities from 2001 to 2019. We document that police unions frequently donate to mayoral candidates—especially in mid-sized and large cities—targeting likely winners and incumbents, and without displaying clear partisan bias. Using a within-city design that accounts for heterogeneous treatment effects in the presence of staggered treatment timing, we find that the election of a police-union-backed mayor leads to an expansion in police department size. However, we do not find improvements in police performance in these cities, suggesting that unions’ political involvement, while providing additional resources, might also be associated with reduced incentives for effort.

shortlist.title: Kuroshio Extension warming shaped by Gulf Stream variability via the Arctic atmosphere
shortlist.abstract: Recent unprecedented ocean warming has produced coherent sea surface temperature anomalies across the Northern Hemisphere extratropics. While the tropical Pacific is a natural source of North Pacific variability, the influence of the mid-latitude North Atlantic has remained poorly understood. Here we investigate whether Gulf Stream variability modulates Kuroshio Extension variability using 100-year idealized model simulations. We find that Gulf Stream variability remotely modulates Kuroshio Extension variability, explaining 13% of its internal sea surface temperature variance, whereas we find no evidence that Kuroshio variability similarly modulates the Gulf Stream. Positive Gulf Stream sea surface temperature anomalies excite a Northern Annular Mode-like atmospheric circulation response that weakens the Aleutian Low over the North Pacific. The resulting northward shift of the Kuroshio Extension enhances northward warm-water transport and promotes warming in the western mid-latitude North Pacific. We further show that a high-resolution ocean model is required to properly capture this coupling between Gulf Stream variability and atmospheric circulation, highlighting the importance of western boundary currents and associated oceanic fronts for this interbasin pathway. These findings indicate that North Atlantic variability contributed to the exceptional North Pacific warming during 2020–2024 and may provide a source of decadal predictability for Northern Hemisphere climate.

shortlist.title: Accretion-powered flares from black hole–disc collisions in galactic nuclei
shortlist.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
shortlist.abstract: Black hole impacts on accretion discs in galactic nuclei can power luminous transients, but predicting their observable signatures is challenging because the post-collision flow is highly time-dependent and inhomogeneous. We present a radiative post-processing framework for relativistic hydrodynamics simulations of black hole–disc collisions. Using physically motivated prescriptions for shock heating, optical depth via an eikonal solver, and photon escape fractions that account for photon trapping and diffusion, we predict light curves and spectral energy distributions over a range of disc densities and collision velocities. Our results indicate that the emission is dominated by the long-lived accretion flow onto the secondary black hole, whose mass supply is highly super-Eddington, rather than by cooling of the unbound ejecta. In the parameter range explored, the luminosity is typically of the order of the Eddington luminosity of the secondary and can reach several times this value, and the emission is generically dominated by soft X-rays. We find that lower velocity collisions produce brighter flares, while the disc surface density mainly controls spectral evolution: low-density discs typically produce ∼keV-peaked flares with weak spectral evolution, whereas high-density discs show softer early emission and late-time hardening. A depletion-time estimate calibrated to our results suggests characteristic durations of hours to days for intermediate-mass secondaries, and yields tflare∝PQPE. We discuss implications for QPE-like transients and for the SMBH-binary candidate OJ 287. Our framework does not include radiative feedback on the gas, therefore the luminosities should be interpreted only as baseline estimates of the available power for radiation.

shortlist.title: Fast, high-fidelity erasure detection of dual-rail qubits with symmetrically coupled readout
shortlist.abstract: Erasure qubits are a promising platform for implementing hardware-efficient quantum error correction. Realizing the error-correction advantages of this encoding requires frequent mid-circuit erasure checks that are fast, high-fidelity, and scalable. Here, we realize erasure detection with a hardware-efficient circuit consisting of a single readout resonator dispersively and symmetrically coupled to both transmons of a dual-rail qubit. We use this circuit to demonstrate single-shot erasure detection in 384 ns with minimal impact on the dual-rail logical manifold, achieving a residual error per check of 6.0(2) × 10⁻⁴, with only 8(3) × 10⁻⁵ induced dephasing per check, and an erasure error per check of 2.54(1)× 10⁻². The high degree of matched dispersive readout coupling (χ-matching) within the dual-rail qubit code space also allows us to realize a new modality: time-continuous erasure detection performed in parallel with single-qubit gates. Here we achieve a median 7.2 × 10⁻⁵ error per gate with < 1 × 10⁻⁵ error induced by erasure detection. This demonstrates a reduction in erasure detection overhead as well as a crucial ingredient for soft information quantum error correction. Together, these results establish symmetrically coupled dispersive readout as a fast, hardware-efficient, and scalable component for erasure-based quantum error correction using transmon dual-rail qubits.

shortlist.title: Daddy’s Girl: Daughters, Managerial Decisions, and Gender Inequality
shortlist.abstract: Using Danish registry data, we study how managers’ gender attitudes shape gender inequality in the workplace by exploiting the birth of a daughter—as opposed to a son—as a plausibly exogenous shock to male managers’ gender attitudes. Comparing within-firm changes in women’s labour outcomes depending on the gender of the manager’s newborn child, we find that women’s relative earnings and employment increase by 4.4% and 2.9%, respectively, following the birth of the manager’s first daughter. These effects are driven by an increase in managers’ propensity to substitute male hires with female hires that have comparable education, hours worked, and earnings. Consistent with this substitution channel, we do not detect any significant effect on firm performance. Because these effects emerge rapidly and persist over time, we can rule out the need for prolonged exposure to gender issues or for personal incentives tied to improving conditions for their own daughters as prerequisites for managers to promote gender equality within their firms.

shortlist.title: Prospects of resolving and localising individual supermassive black hole binaries with pulsar timing arrays: the host ranking challenge
shortlist.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
shortlist.abstract: Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs) are soon expected to detect individually resolved supermassive black hole (SMBH) binaries, opening the possibility for multi-messenger discoveries. The biggest challenge will be to pinpoint the host galaxy in a large localisation area. We simulate realistic binary populations consistent with the gravitational wave (GW) background, projecting the PTA sensitivity for the next 0-10 years. We inject the loudest binary on top of the background and use a standard detection pipelines to constrain its properties. We cross-match the GW sky map with comprehensive all-sky galaxy catalogues and estimate the number of candidate hosts in the localisation area assessing, for the first time, the number of missing galaxies due to incomplete coverage. We develop a ranking system that excludes galaxies with properties inconsistent with the GW posteriors, and prioritizes the remaining galaxies for follow-up observations. We find a ≈21, ≈38 and ≈51 percent probability of resolving a binary in the next 0, 5 and 10 years, respectively, reduced to 0.3, 3.8 and 14.1 percent if we consider only sources potentially localisable within 2,000 deg2. The localisation areas span hundreds of square degrees, but shrink significantly with the addition of more data. They contain on average ≈190,000 early type galaxies and ≈40,000 active galactic nuclei, with ≈33,500 missing candidate hosts. Our ranking method can exclude about 37 percent of the potential hosts and efficiently rank those remaining when the galaxy catalogue provides SMBH masses and redshifts, but becomes more inefficient when it relies on apparent magnitudes.

shortlist.title: Joint single-cell capture of Cas9 edits and transcriptomes reveals on- and off-target effects on gene expression
shortlist.abstract: A longstanding barrier in genome engineering with CRISPR-Cas9 has been the inability to measure editing outcomes and their functional effects at single-cell resolution. Here we present Superb-seq, which captures single-cell edits and transcriptome effects by integrating Cas9 editing, T7 in situ transcription and single-cell RNA sequencing. We performed Superb-seq on 35,000 cells from three cell lines. Using seven guide RNAs to target four chromatin remodeler genes in 10,000 K562 cells, Superb-seq detected 5,761 edited cells, all on-target sites and 36 off-target sites. Superb-seq improved estimation of downstream perturbation effects on gene expression compared to Perturb-seq. We compared Superb-seq to 4 bulk off-target detection methods and identified between 6 and 210 edit sites across 3 benchmarking guides. Nineteen off-target edits were associated with differential gene expression, nine of which were cell type-specific. In summary, Superb-seq illuminates the consequences of Cas9 genome editing by connecting single-cell edits with changes in gene expression.

shortlist.title: Cubic-equivariant neural density functional theory for three-dimensional lattice fluids
shortlist.abstract: We construct a neural classical density functional that acts directly on unrestricted three-dimensional density profiles. As a computationally tractable test bed, we consider parallel hard cubes of side length three on a simple cubic lattice. A fully convolutional network learns the one-body direct-correlation functional c⁽¹⁾[ρ] from data obtained with grand-canonical Monte Carlo simulations in randomized external potentials. Complete profiles are used during both training and inference; a stochastic Bernoulli mask on the output sites makes full-profile training effective without explicitly extracting and storing overlapping local density windows. Averaging the first-layer kernels over all 48 rotations and reflections of the cubic point group additionally imposes exact cubic equivariance without data augmentation. We compare the learned functional with independent simulation data and with the lattice fundamental-measure functional of Lafuente and Cuesta. The neural functional markedly improves the homogeneous equation of state and the density profile at a planar hard wall. For the anisotropic pair distribution around a fixed particle, both functionals reproduce the principal packing shells, with their relative accuracy depending on crystallographic direction. These results demonstrate neural density-functional calculations on complete three-dimensional profiles while also identifying accurate full-dimensional training data, thermodynamic consistency, and structural correlations as the central challenges for extensions to continuum fluids.

shortlist.title: Echidna: a Bayesian framework for integrative inference of copy number alterations impacting phenotypic plasticity
shortlist.abstract: The ability of cells to adapt their behavior in response to genetic or environmental changes is a fundamental biological process that drives cellular diversity in both normal and pathological contexts, including in tumor evolution. Copy number alterations (CNAs), which can include large-scale changes in genomic ploidy, play a key role in creating adaptive advantages in evolving cell populations. However, tracing these populations across experiments and disentangling the role of CNAs from other sources of transcriptional variability remains challenging and expensive. Here we present Echidna, a Bayesian hierarchical model that integrates single-cell RNA sequencing and bulk whole-genome sequencing data to enable robust integrative inference of CNAs, jointly across samples and treatment time points, to better understand the impact of genomic events on cellular phenotype. Applying Echidna to patient tumor specimens, we demonstrate its superior performance in clonal reconstruction and derive insights into therapy resistance mechanisms.

shortlist.title: An open agentic AI co-scientist for clinical and biomedical discovery
shortlist.abstract: Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer’s blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. To support research involving sensitive clinical datasets, OpenScientist can operate in a fully air-gapped environment using open-source models for inference. OpenScientist demonstrates that open, auditable, agentic AI can support real-world clinical research by researching the literature, generating hypotheses, executing analyses, and generating insights from complex datasets.

shortlist.title: Integrated QTL mapping and CRISPR screening in pooled iPSC-derived microglia reveals genetic drivers of neurodegenerative risk
shortlist.abstract: Mounting evidence implicates microglia in neurodegeneration, but linking disease-associated genetic variants to target genes and cellular phenotypes is hindered by the inaccessibility of these cells. We differentiated 261 human induced pluripotent stem cell lines into microglia-like (iMGL) cells in pools with phenotypic (differentiation, phagocytosis and migration) and single-cell transcriptomic readouts. Burden analysis of deleterious variants detected 36 genes influencing microglial phenotypes. Expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analysis identified 7,121 eQTL-associated genes and 79 colocalizations across four neurodegenerative disease genome-wide association studies, half of which had limited prior evidence of causality. Integration of eQTL and phenotypic associations highlighted the role of disease-relevant variants, including LRRK2 and TREM2 acting through microglial phagocytosis. A coupled CRISPR screen identified a role for TREM2 in phagocytosis and highlighted the importance of cell type in the directionality of phenotypic effects. By contextualizing variant effects within iMGLs in different inflammatory states, we provide a comprehensive framework for interpreting the function of risk loci in neurodegenerative disorders.

shortlist.title: Enhancing Gradient Inversion Attacks in Federated Learning via Hierarchical Feature Optimization
shortlist.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
shortlist.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a compelling paradigm for privacy-preserving distributed machine learning, allowing multiple clients to collaboratively train a global model by transmitting locally computed gradients to a central server without exposing their private data. Nonetheless, recent studies find that the gradients exchanged in the FL system are also vulnerable to privacy leakage, e.g., an attacker can invert shared gradients to reconstruct sensitive data by leveraging pre-trained generative adversarial networks (GAN) as prior knowledge. However, existing attacks simply perform gradient inversion in the latent space of the GAN model, which limits their expression ability and generalizability. To tackle these challenges, we propose Gradient Inversion over Feature Domains (GIFD), which disassembles the GAN model and searches the hierarchical features of the intermediate layers. Instead of optimizing only over the initial latent code, we progressively change the optimized layer, from the initial latent space to intermediate layers closer to the output images. In addition, we design a regularizer to avoid unreal image generation by adding a small l₁ ball constraint to the searching range. We also extend GIFD to the out-of-distribution (OOD) setting, which weakens the assumption that the training sets of GANs and FL tasks obey the same data distribution. Furthermore, we consider the challenging OOD scenario of label inconsistency and propose a label mapping technique as an effective solution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can achieve high-quality reconstruction and outperform competitive baselines across a variety of FL scenarios.

shortlist.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
shortlist.abstract: A central goal of current Spiking Neural Network (SNN) research is to improve their accuracy toward becoming low-power alternatives to Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). This work further argues that realizing this ambition requires improving not only accuracy but also robustness, defined as the ability to maintain correct predictions under input perturbations. We identify two key issues in existing SNN methods that undermine robustness. First, binary spiking activations can produce large activation-state changes under small perturbations. Second, the lack of effective weight constraints makes network outputs more sensitive to input variations. To this end, we propose Burst Spiking Neural Networks (BuSNNs), built upon Burst-enhanced Spiking Neurons (BSNs) and a Dynamic Weight Constraint (DWC) mechanism. BSNs incorporate burst firing to provide a graded spiking pattern. This spiking mechanism mitigates perturbation-induced transitions in activation states and thereby enhances robustness. DWC penalizes connection weights based on activation states, effectively reducing weight magnitudes and improving robustness while preserving accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses to support these robustness effects. Experimental results further show that, on smaller-scale benchmarks such as CIFAR-10, BuSNNs outperform both SNN and ANN counterparts in accuracy and robustness. On large-scale ImageNet, BuSNN with the MS ResNet-34 backbone further improves top-1 accuracy and corruption robustness over the corresponding SNN baseline by 3.18% and 2.66%, respectively. Despite using spike-based activations, BuSNNs surpass 4-bit activation-quantized ANN baselines and approach 8-bit ANN baselines on ImageNet. They also preserve SNNs' low-power advantage with up to a 4.38× theoretical energy…

shortlist.title: Maternal and early life obesity programs CD4+ T cell fate to impair vaccine immunity
shortlist.abstract: In their first 3 years, children experience an average of 14 infections and receive vaccines against roughly 15 pathogens, yet whether maternal and early life obesity alters adaptive immune responses during this critical period remains largely undefined. Using a mouse model that mirrored the epidemiological link between maternal and childhood obesity, we found that high-fat diet exposure during pregnancy or early postnatal life, but not adulthood, reshaped the epigenetic and transcriptional landscape of naive CD4+ T cells and impaired their ability to differentiate into T follicular helper (TFH) cells and support germinal center reactions in response to mRNA-based and protein-based vaccines. Mechanistically, epigenetic repression of the ubiquitin-editing enzyme A20 (Tnfaip3) was a central driver of these defects. Pediatric patients with haploinsufficiency of A20 displayed a marked reduction in circulating TFH cells. Altogether, these findings establish maternal and early life obesity as determinants of adaptive immunity during a critical developmental window. Henao-Mejia and colleagues show that a high-fat diet during pregnancy or early postnatal life impairs CD4+ TFH cell differentiation and germinal center reactions in response to vaccination in young mice.

shortlist.title: Multimodal omics identifies a lymphoid-biased multipotent progenitor population with limited age-associated remodeling
shortlist.abstract: Hematopoietic aging is marked by declining regenerative capacity and a shift from lymphoid to myeloid output. Previous studies have focused primarily on hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), yet whether aging uniformly remodels the hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) compartment, or selectively affects distinct populations, remains largely unknown. To address this, we profile HSCs and multipotent progenitors MPP1-6 from young and aged mice across transcriptomic, epigenomic, metabolomic and lipidomic layers, together with single-cell division and in vivo serial transplantation assays. We identify young MPP6 (negative for CD150, CD34, CD48 and CD135) as an HSC-like, lymphoid-biased population with long-term reconstitution capacity, positioned within the top-tier of the differentiation hierarchy and marked by low global chromatin accessibility and metabolic activity. Upon aging, MPP6 preserved long-term lymphoid reconstitution, underwent limited transcriptional and regulatory remodeling, and did not accumulate polyunsaturated phospholipids or show mitochondrial oxidation. By contrast, most HSPCs, and particularly HSCs, underwent pronounced age-associated changes, including myeloid-biased expansion, metabolic rewiring, extensive distal regulatory alteration and accumulation of long-chain polyunsaturated phospholipids linked to increased oxidative stress. Pseudotime analysis further resolved the aged MPP6 compartment into two subsets, including a dormant, lymphoid-biased Dlk1-expressing population characterized by reduced mitochondrial activity, which was distinctly affected by inflammatory challenge in vivo. Together, these findings establish MPP6 as a comparatively resilient population within the aged HSPC compartment and suggest that it may represent a potential…

shortlist.title: HOPO 14-1, an Oral Actinide Chelator: A Phase 1 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
shortlist.abstract: Importance: Current treatments approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for internal actinide contamination (pentetate calcium trisodium and pentetate zinc trisodium) require intravenous injection or nebulized inhalation under medical supervision and have limited radionuclide coverage. HOPO 14-1, an oral form of 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO), is the first shelf-stable, broad-spectrum actinide chelator in clinical development that does not require intravenous access or trained personnel. In preclinical models, 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO) removed a broad range of actinides, and its oral route supports scalable emergency medical use. Objective: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetic parameters, and excretion of a single dose of HOPO 14-1 in healthy adults. Participants were recruited and screened between March 2023 and July 2025 and follow-up was completed in August 2025. shortlist.title: Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
shortlist.abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Consistent with diagnostic expectation theory, higher exposure to Ebola fear does not result in a significant learning effect during the COVID-19 pandemic. shortlist.title: Revisiting Overestimation Bias of Q-learning: Breaking Bias Propagation Chains Does Well
shortlist.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
shortlist.abstract: This paper revisits the overestimation bias of Q-learning from a new perspective, i.e., the breaking bias propagation chains. We make five-fold contributions. First, we analyze the estimation bias propagation chains of Q-learning, and find that the bias propagated from previous steps dominates the maximum Q-value estimation bias and slows the convergence speed, instead of the current bias. Second, we propose a novel positive-negative bias alternating algorithm called Alternating Q-learning (AQ). It breaks the unidirectional estimation bias propagation chains via alternately executing Q-learning and Double Q-learning. We show theoretically that there exist suitable alternating parameters to eliminate the propagation bias. Third, we design an adaptive alternating strategy for AQ, obtaining Adaptive Alternating Q-learning (AdaAQ). It applies a softmax strategy with the absolute value of TD error to choose Q-learning or Double Q-learning for each state-action pair. Fourth, we extend AQ and AdaAQ to the large-scale settings with function approximation, i.e., including both discrete- and continuous-action Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). Fifth, both discrete-and continuous-action DRL experiments show that our method outperforms several state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines drastically; tabular MDP experiments reveal fundamental insights into why our method can achieve superior performance.

shortlist.title: Long-term development of a motor memory
shortlist.abstract: Human behaviour is developed through continuous adaptation to our environment over a range of timescales. Extensive studies have investigated the mechanisms and computations underlying this process of sensorimotor adaptation using several hundred trials. However, most of our motor skills have had countless hours of practice. Here we study a simple motor adaptation task using thousands of training trials over multiple weeks to study the long-term development of a motor memory, and examine changes in adaptation, retention, interlimb transfer, decay, spontaneous recovery and generalization. Unlike previous studies, participants showed near complete compensation to the novel dynamics, along with long-term increases in retention and spontaneous recovery. Moreover, we find narrowing in the angular generalization, suggesting continual tuning of the motor memory to the task. This demonstrates the extensive changes occurring with longer training of motor tasks, highlighting their importance in studies of sensorimotor control, rehabilitation and training.

shortlist.title: Long-Term Survival After Initial Invasive or Conservative Management of Stable Coronary Disease in ISCHEMIA-EXTEND
shortlist.abstract: Importance: It is unknown whether routine invasive management of chronic coronary disease improves long-term survival when added to guideline-directed medical therapy. Objective: To compare the effects of initial invasive and conservative strategies on long-term mortality in patients with chronic coronary disease. Design, Setting, and Participants: In this long-term follow-up study of the International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness with Medical and Invasive Approaches (ISCHEMIA), an international trial of patients with chronic coronary disease, moderate or severe ischemia, left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or more, and no left main coronary artery disease, unacceptable angina, or recent acute coronary syndrome, participants were randomized at 320 sites in 37 countries beginning August 2012 and followed up through December 2025. Data were analyzed using the intention-to-treat principle. Intervention: ISCHEMIA randomized patients to an initial invasive strategy of guideline-directed medical therapy plus coronary angiography and revascularization (when feasible) or an initial conservative strategy with guideline-directed medical therapy alone, with invasive management for failure of medical therapy. Main Outcomes and Measures: All-cause, cardiovascular, and noncardiovascular mortality were analyzed using cumulative incidence estimates, Cox and Fine-Gray models, bayesian analysis, and restricted mean survival time. Results: Among 5179 participants, median age was 64 (IQR, 58-70) years; 23% were female, 42% had diabetes, and median ejection fraction was 60% (IQR, 55%-65%). During 9-year median follow-up (range, 1 day to 13.4 years), 1071 deaths occurred (782 during extended follow-up): 672 cardiovascular, 359 noncardiovascular, and 40 unclassified.…

shortlist.title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
shortlist.abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. shortlist.title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation
shortlist.abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Fahlenbrach gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Swiss Finance Institute. shortlist.title: Hemodynamic spectral signatures across vigilance states: a whole-night EEG/fNIRS investigation
shortlist.abstract: Sleep is accompanied by coordinated changes in neuronal activity and cerebral hemodynamics. However, cortical hemodynamic signatures across sleep stages remain poorly characterized, partly because most human electroencephalography (EEG)/functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies are limited in duration, rarely capture deep or Rapid-Eye-Movement (REM) sleep, have low sampling rate, or rely on a sleep-deprivation paradigm, which limits the generalizability of findings. Here, we combined whole-night polysomnography, EEG and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) in healthy young adults, as a bedside technology to monitor cortical hemodynamic fluctuations. We recorded fNIRS using an optimal, personalized, locally dense bilateral frontoparietal montage, alongside peripheral physiology recordings (respiration, photoplethysmography, mean arterial pressure). We computed oscillatory components of oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin (HbO-HbR) spectra across sleep stages using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Additionally, we analyzed within the same regions an independent sleep EEG-fMRI dataset (no REM recorded). Our results are suggesting that across frontal and parietal regions, slow-frequency (0.002-0.1Hz) power increased during N1 sleep in HbO and then progressively attenuated across N2 and N3 sleep, in HbO, HbR, and fMRI. REM showed a re-emergence of very-low-frequency power (<0.01Hz) in HbO and HbR. Higher-frequency oscillations (0.15-0.5Hz; overlapping respiratory-band) were selectively enhanced during NREM sleep (largest increase during N3) and returned toward wake-like levels during REM in frontal regions, with regional differences. Peripheral signals captured systemic physiology oscillations but did not reproduce the cortical stage-specific patterns.…

fundamentals.title: Operator structure of power corrections and anomalous scaling in energy correlators
fundamentals.abstract: Energy correlators offer a clean probe of quantum chromodynamics, serving as an ideal laboratory to rigorously investigate non-perturbative power corrections. The recent discovery that linear corrections exhibit a universal anomalous scaling points to a deep, underlying theoretical structure. We uncover the quantum field-theoretic origin of this phenomenon in the energy-energy correlator using light-ray operators. Through an explicit loop calculation, we derive the one-loop anomalous dimension, revealing that the dijet operator must be combined with a specific triple-jet component. This provides a first-principles framework that connects operator theory with high-precision collider phenomenology.
fundamentals.topic: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

fundamentals.title: Unified theory of quartz tuning fork resonators
fundamentals.abstract: Quartz tuning forks, functioning as electrically driven piezoelectric resonators, have long served as exceptionally stable and widely adopted timing references in diverse domains of research and industry. Yet, experimentally measured electrical resonance spectra often exhibit resonance evolutions that remain unexplained within existing theoretical descriptions. Here we develop a unified continuum electromechanical modal framework that integrates piezoelectric electrodynamics, variational structural dynamics, and symmetry-selected electromechanical observability. Our theory shows quantitative agreement with experimental results, demonstrating that electrical observability emerges not from the underlying mechanical eigenmodes alone. The resulting framework unifies conventional coupled-oscillator, equivalent-circuit, and continuum descriptions within a single first-principles theory and provides a rigorous basis for precision electromechanical characterization.

fundamentals.title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
fundamentals.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
fundamentals.abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub-grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert-vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub-grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity…

fundamentals.title: Optimal learning of quantum channels in diamond distance
fundamentals.abstract: The evolution of quantum states can be described by quantum channels. The task of estimating an unknown quantum channel, known as process tomography, is a central problem in quantum information theory. A long-standing open question is how many uses of an unknown channel are required to learn it to a precision quantified by the standard metric for distinguishing quantum processes, known as the diamond distance. Here we address this by establishing the query complexity of channel tomography with optimal dependence on the dimensions of the input and output spaces and the channel’s Kraus rank at any fixed constant accuracy in diamond distance. We design an algorithm that establishes an upper bound and prove a matching lower bound for learning a channel to the given accuracy. Our algorithm follows the strategy of performing optimal tomography on the Choi-state representation of the process, and we show that channel tomography can be reduced to the well-studied problem of pure-state tomography. As channels subsume states, unitaries and measurements as special cases, our protocol provides a unified framework for tomography of these tasks.

fig.label: Figure 1
fig.caption: Protocol for learning quantum channels. Parallel invocations of the unknown channel Λ , applied to halves of maximally entangled states |Ω⟩ , prepare copies of its normalised Choi state Φ_c=J(Λ) . A purification channel then maps these Choi-state copies to copies of a random purification |Φ_c⟩ , which are learned using a sample-optimal pure-state tomography scheme. Finally, a classical post-processing step, formulated as a semidefinite program projecting onto the set of CPTP maps, returns a channel estimate Λ̂ satisfying ‖Λ̂-Λ‖_◇≤ε with high probability.

fundamentals.title: In-plane orbital magnetization with layer hybridization
fundamentals.abstract: The modern theory of orbital magnetization successfully describes the response of Bloch electrons to magnetic fields in fully periodic crystals, but it does not directly address the distinct regime of an in-plane field in multilayer systems with layer hybridization. Coherent interlayer tunneling allows electrons to form circulating current loops, producing an in-plane orbital response that is absent in strictly two-dimensional limit and qualitatively different from the conventional three-dimensional one. Here we develop a theory of in-plane orbital magnetization for this {} regime, where the layer thickness is comparable to the vertical mean free path. Starting from the current-loop picture, we construct the in-plane orbital angular momentum operator and derive exact expressions for the orbital magnetic moment and the in-plane orbital magnetic susceptibility. As a concrete physical application, we predict a gate-tunable in-plane orbital magnetoelectric effect in layered materials. Our framework establishes a general foundation for in-plane orbital responses and suggests new opportunities for orbitronics in layer-hybridized quantum materials.

fundamentals.title: Sound propagation in striped supersolid gases at zero temperature
fundamentals.abstract: The role of dimensionality in the identification of sound modes in many-body systems characterized by the spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry is a topic of high interdisciplinary interest in both classical and quantum systems. The emergence of stripes in superfluids is a particularly interesting example where the dimensionality of the system differs from the one of the crystal phase. Here we present a unified hydrodynamic approach for the sound propagation in the stripe phase realized in ultracold dipolar and spin-orbit-coupled Bose gases at zero temperature. Despite the deep difference of the two platforms at a microscopic level, a similar hydrodynamic description can be formulated at a macroscopic level. The main difference between the two platforms is the lack of Galilean invariance in the spin-orbit case, resulting in a different identification of the normal (non-superfluid) component of the density. In both cases the spectrum comprises two sounds, reflecting the spontaneous breaking of the U(1) and translational symmetries. Both sounds exhibit an anisotropic behavior. A comparison with the first and second sounds of the smectic-A liquid crystal is also presented.
